Manasseh said this, and many others, of whom it is written: “And they sacrificed their sons, and their daughters, to devils.” Or surely, as some say, it is the voice of the demons to the people: O you peoples, sacrifice men.
**“men”** — or accusative
13.3:
**“Therefore they shall be as a morning cloud”**
• because they sacrifice men to calves
• Allegorically: The heretics are compared to cloud, dew and dust; of whom it is written: “These are … clouds without water.” For they have the look of the prophetic and apostolic clouds to which the truth of God came, but they have not the waters, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit.
**“as a … cloud”** — Cloud and dew are put to flight when the sun comes; dust and smoke dissolve into the thin air. So as these four things quickly vanish, so they will quickly be led away to the Assyrians. Hence above: “Samaria hath made her king to pass as froth upon the face of the water.”
**“and as the early dew that passeth away, as the dust that is driven with a whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney”**
• through which the smoke goes out
• Chimney: the house of smoke.
13.4:
**“But I am the Lord thy God from the land of Egypt”**
• understand: I was, from the time when “I brought thee out of the land of Egypt.”
• Allegorically: The Lord led the heretics out of the darkness of unbelief, where they once served Pharaoh and his captains, and commanded that in the Church they should know no other God but him who creates and saves. And he feeds them so that they can say: The Lord feedeth me, and I shall want nothing; and he gives them the bread “which came down from heaven,” which they had not eaten in Egypt, and waters from Christ the rock. But, filled with the bread of the Scriptures, they lifted up their heart against the Creator and fashioned another god, ascribing whatever they had eaten and drunk to their own merits and not to God. They forgot God, who had commanded them to bind the words of the law before their eyes and to have them in their hands, so that they should never forget their God.
• They were ungrateful to the giver through so great a wilderness, where there is neither corn nor trees, neither vines nor grass, nor water to temper the heat of the sun: for forty years Israel could not have reached the land of the Jordan unless the Lord had supplied everything.
**“But I”** — As above, so here he recounts what he did for that people.
**“and thou shalt know no God but me”** — “there is no God, besides me.”
**“and there is no saviour beside me”** — who can save
13.5:
**“I knew thee”** — that is, I loved and chose
**“in the desert”** — where I fed thee
**“in the land of the wilderness”** — where there was want of all things
13.6:
**“According to their pastures they were filled, and were made full”** — and yet I gave them manna from heaven, springs from the rock; hence: “He grew fat, and thick and gross.”
**“and”** — yet
**“they lifted up their heart, and have forgotten me”** — who gave so much
13.7:
**“And”** — therefore
**“I will be to them”**
• to them, ungrateful
• They are of such iniquity that even when placed in captivity they will deservedly feel my severity, lest they ascribe their miseries to the strength of their enemies.
**“And I will be”** — When they have been handed over to their enemies, I, who was always most merciful towards them, will turn on them with the fierceness of all the beasts. And this fits not only the Israelites, who are held in the mountains of the Medes for idolatry, but also the heretics, who out of pride of mind fashioned the novelty of a false doctrine and, forgetting their God, followed strange gods.
**“as a lioness”** — which is most savage when her whelps are snatched away, as is the leopard
**“as a leopard in the way of the Assyrians”** — when they are led away captive by the Assyrians
13.8:
**“I will meet them as a bear that is robbed of her whelps”** — than which nothing is said to be more savage when she has lost her whelps or wants food
**“and I will rend”** — by the Assyrians
**“the inner parts”** — I will take away the vital parts of their heart
**“of their liver: and I will devour them there as a lion”** — as a lion devours its prey
**“the beast of the field”** — Sennacherib, or the devil, who dwells in the desert of the world
**“shall tear them”** — is at hand
13.9:
**“Destruction is thy own, O Israel”**
• that is, thou thyself art the cause of thy destruction
• Every heretic is lost, and there is no help for him in anything but in the mercy of God alone, if he repents. His king and judges are the devil and the demons, or the heresiarchs, who in the time of distress will not be able to deliver him; who were given in wrath, and will be taken away in indignation: not that the Lord wished them to have such kings, for he will not take away what he had freely given; but he had left them to their own pleasures.
**“Destruction is thy own”** — He speaks ironically to those who, against the will of God, chose themselves a king, by whose strength they boasted they would be victors. So he says: The king of whom thou didst promise thyself that he would fight thy wars, let him save thee now above all, when danger threatens from the Assyrians; but thou hast no man for king, thou who hast cast me, God, away.
**“only in me”** — not from thyself, or from anyone else
**“thy help is”** — if thou doest penance
13.10:
**“Where is thy king?”** — Jeroboam, or even Saul
**“now especially let him save thee in all thy cities”** — such as the counts and the other princes under the kings
**“and thy judges, of whom thou saidst: Give me kings and princes”** — where are they? why do they not come to thy help?
13.11:
**“I will give thee a king”** — As if to say: I answered: I will give thee a king.
**“in my wrath”** — So that in the days of harvest I showed rain, against the custom of Palestine: a king, that is, Saul; and I will take away in my indignation Zedekiah, who, with his eyes put out, was led to Babylon. Or Jeroboam was the king given in wrath, and the one taken away in indignation was Hoshea, the last of the kings of the ten tribes.
13.12:
**“The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up, his sin is hidden”**
• not from God, to whom all things are open, but from himself, who would not keep it in mind
• When the last captivity comes, and his iniquity is made plain to all, then he will be tormented with sudden pains like a woman in labour.
• The heretics have their iniquity bound up, which they have spoken on high, and their sins are hidden, because they think to hide the poison of their heart; but when the day of tribulation comes it will be laid open with pains and wailings. “He is an unwise son,” who has forsaken the wisdom of God, and in the breach of the children he has killed he will not be able to bear the wrath of God.
**“is bound up”** — As what is tied up in a bag is kept so as not to be lost, so the iniquity by which Ephraim sinned against God stays as it were bound up until the day of captivity; and this because his sin is hidden.
13.13:
**“The sorrows of a woman in labour shall come upon him”** — for
**“he is … son”** — “Israel is my son, my first-born.”
**“an unwise”** — for he did not know the true father
**“for now”** — when the captivity has come
**“he shall not stand in the breach of the children”** — he will not be able to bear the tribulation of the children, who will be killed before their fathers; or he shall not stand, but will be led away captive
13.14:
**“I will deliver them out of the hand of death”**
• from the work of sin, which draws to death; hence it is said: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue”; or the hand of death is the power of the devil
• Death is when the soul is separated from the body; hell is the place where souls are shut up, either for refreshment or for punishment.
• Whatever separates the love of brotherhood is hell.
**“out of the hand of death”** — The Lord speaks to those whom he deigns to set free by his grace.
**“from death”** — from hell
**“I will redeem”** — with the price of my blood
**“them”** — the Jews or the Gentiles who believe, or even the heretics who come to their senses; hence he adds: I will be thy death
**“O death, I will be thy death”** — by dying I will destroy thee
**“I will be thy bite”** — By bringing out my elect and leaving the reprobate there. Or death and hell are the devil, whom Christ bit so that he should lose his power, not so that he should cease to exist altogether.
**“O hell”** — in whose jaws all were swallowed up
**“comfort”** — The most merciful Father, seeing that by the sentence pronounced “in Adam all die,” says: I cannot have comfort, because the whole human race is rushing into death. Or the prophet himself, seeing that by the common necessity he is to die and go down to hell, says: I cannot be comforted, and whatever I conceive in my mind cannot soften my grief, while I see the inescapable necessity of death.
**“comfort is hidden from my eyes”** — Some, according to the history of that time, speak of the two brothers divided from each other, Israel and Judah; so that what was then figured in part may now be felt in the whole, and Israel is to be redeemed and Judah set free with the whole human race.
13.15:
**“Because he”** — hell
**“shall make a separation between brothers”** — while it receives one, it leaves the other surviving
**“will bring a burning wind”**
• The Son, who takes away sins; of whom Habakkuk: “God will come from the south, and the holy one from Mount Pharan.”
• From the desert of the human race, in which the devil, seeking rest, found none. Or from the womb of the Virgin, who conceived without the seed of man; and from the simple and pure rod rose up the flower that makes us rise up with him.
• All these things happened to the Jews in the time of the captivity, when they were either killed or led away into perpetual servitude.
• Having bound the strong one, he carried with him into paradise the saints who were in hell, like precious vessels; or the vessels which the devil before longed to hold, he took away.
**“will bring”** — The burning wind is the word of the Church, which dries up the shoots of all the heretics, and plunders and scatters those who had been gathered in death by the heretics’ teaching.
**“the Lord”** — the Father
**“that shall rise from the desert”** — from the lowliness of the cross to the heights
**“and it shall dry up … springs”** — sins
**“his”** — of death
**“and shall make his fountain desolate”** — the devil, or sins; when these are dried up, death itself will be dried up
13.16:
the voice of the prophet, not so much cursing as foretelling
**“Let Samaria perish, because she hath stirred up her God to bitterness”**
• by worshipping idols they drove him who was sweet and kind to vengeance
• therefore
• Allegorically: Let the heretics perish, who boast that they keep the commandments of God, and, though they are most unclean, call themselves clean, denying the penance by which sins are cleansed. For whatever they say fights against God, and they make the merciful one cruel to themselves. Or so that those who ought to be perfect men may be cut down by the spiritual sword, as little ones that are to be dashed against the rock, of which it is said: “Blessed be he that shall take and dash thy little ones against the rock.” Her women with child too, who have conceived of evil seed, will be ripped up, so that they may not bear the worst of sons.
**“Let Samaria perish”** — The warriors of Samaria will be killed, the sucklings dashed, the women with child ripped up; so that, when the evil seed perishes and the cockle is burnt, only the wheat may remain, to be stored in God’s barn.
**“by the sword”** — understand: of the Assyrians
**“let them perish …, let their little ones be dashed”** — that is, crushed on the ground
**“and let the women with child be ripped up”** — let the women with child be ripped up by the sword unto death

14.1:
**“Return, O Israel”**
• from the ungodliness of idolatry
• so that thou perish not
• In the moral sense: Let the soul that has fallen into sins rise up to penance, bringing forth “fruits worthy of penance,” and turn back from evil works.
**“Return”** — Having foretold the calamities that threatened the ten tribes for idolatry, the prophet now turns to them and gives them counsel to repent and pray to God.
**“to the Lord thy God”** — whose making thou art, to whom thou owest service
**“for thou hast fallen down by thy iniquity”** — thou hast fallen by idolatry; rise up by the worship of God
14.2:
**“Take with you words”** — bring forth prayers and a true confession of your sins
**“Take”** — Having exhorted them to penance, he teaches them how to pour out their prayers to God.
**“and return”** — as much in words as in works
**“to the Lord”** — who is the true physician
**“and say to him: Take away all iniquity”**
• every one of the faithful ought to say such things
• Allegorically: The calves of the lips are the confession of the Holy Trinity, and of the Incarnation, the Passion and the Resurrection. “For, with the heart, we believe unto justice: but, with the mouth, confession is made unto salvation.” He who offers this victim does not hope in the king of the Assyrians. So it is said to the heretics: Return to God, you who have fallen by falsehood. Take with you the words of faith and confession, and say to God: Take away the iniquity that dwells in our heart, and receive the good confession; and so we will render the victim of our lips by praising thee and giving thanks; and we will not ride through pride upon horses, that is, upon those whom we begot in error; and we will no more say to the work of our hands, that is, to the doctrine we put together with crafty eloquence: Thou art our God. And he who returns to God in this way appeases the loving Father.
**“all”** — Leave nothing of sickness, nothing of the former ruin, lest the shoots of the evil seed spring up again; and when thou hast taken away the evil, we shall be able to offer the good. The carnal victims being rejected, the victim that appeases God is a pure confession.
**“and receive the good”** — confession, prayers, thanksgiving
**“and we will render the calves of our lips”** — “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit”; the carnal victims being rejected, the victim that appeases God is a pure confession
14.3:
**“Assyria shall not save us”** — from now on we put our hope not in the Assyrians but in thee, who art the true helper
**“we will not ride upon horses”** — of the Egyptians, who had swift horses; but “vain is the horse for safety”
**“neither will we say any more: The works of our hands are our gods”** — that is, we will no more worship the works of our hands, namely, the calves
**“for thou wilt have mercy on … that is in thee”** — that is, thou wilt have mercy, as a loving father, on the people of Israel, which had lost thee by unbelief, when it returns to thee
**“the people”**
• or: the fatherless
• The fatherless: because he withdrew from his evil father the devil, and so is saved. Or the people of Israel, of which it is said: “Israel is my son, my first-born.”
14.4:
**“I will heal their breaches”** — I will forgive the sins by which they have been broken and wounded
**“I will heal”** — God answers those who return to the Father by penance. This passage we can refer both to the ten tribes then, and now, at the coming of Christ, to the Jews, and to the heretics and to the Gentiles; for whoever do penance will obtain pardon. And it is to be noted that the salvation of Israel, its return to God and its redemption from captivity are to be taken not carnally, as the Jews think, but spiritually, as is most truly proved.
**“I will love them”** — I love those who love me
**“freely”** — of mercy alone, for “God first hath loved us”
**“for … is turned away”** — through penance
**“my wrath”** — which was for their sins
**“from them”** — and
14.5:
**“I will be as the dew”**
• steeped in this dew
• for I will take away the heat of the burning fire and of lust
**“Israel shall spring as the lily”** — imitating the lily, who said: “I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the vallies.”
**“and his root shall shoot forth as that of Libanus”**
• that is, the good will will be brought to the doing of the good work
• The trees of Libanus are tall: as far as they lift their tops into the air, so far they sink their roots into the depths, so that no storm moves them.
• Because he had said: his root shall shoot forth as that of Libanus, lest we think he speaks of cedars and fruitless trees, he compares the man converted to God to the fruitful olive, of which it is said elsewhere: “But I, as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.” This olive has a smell like that of Libanus, or of frankincense, so that he can say: “We are unto God the good odour of Christ.” Its fruit the wise virgins made ready; it soothes swelling, refreshes weary limbs, gives light in darkness, and anoints those who strive in the contest.
14.6:
**“shall spread”** — “they shall go from virtue to virtue”
**“His branches”** — on which God’s birds rest
**“and his glory shall be as the olive tree”** — That is, he is made rich by the works of mercy, which are signified by the oil, and, his lamp being lit, he shines in the darkness, giving others an example of working well.
**“and his smell as that of Libanus”** — Libanus among the Greeks and Hebrews is the name of a mountain and of frankincense; here it stands for frankincense. For as we are delighted by the smell of frankincense, so by the good report of a just man. Or, if it stands for the mountain, Libanus is a most fertile mountain, covered with the thickest foliage of trees.
14.7:
**“They shall be converted that sit under his shadow”**
• Those who first withdrew from the Father and afterwards were converted receive this reward: that they sit under his shadow, that is, dwell under his protection.
• and
**“They shall be converted”** — Or they shall live upon wheat, that is, upon the body and blood of the Lord; or they shall live in everlasting happiness through him who is the true corn.
**“they shall live”** — who had been dead
**“upon wheat”** — abundance of all things
**“and they shall blossom”** — As if to say: the elect blossom with good works, like Christ, who is the true vine.
**“his memorial”** — The wine of Libanus can be called wine seasoned with divers spices, so that it gives off a sweet smell. For as spiced wine smells sweet, so does the memory of a just man who imitates God by good works. Or the wine of Libanus is that which was offered to God in the temple. For as he delighted in the wine that was offered him, so he rejoices in the fragrance that comes from the faith and works of believers.
14.8:
**“Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols?”**
• As if to say: Since thou art to receive such good things from penance, why, O Ephraim, dost thou set idols before me any more?
• Ephraim: that is, every penitent; thou who hast begun to be mine by penance, despise idols from now on.
**“I will hear him”** — I who humbled him when he turned away will receive him when he repents
**“and I will make him flourish”** — I will make him walk the right way through me
**“like a green fir tree”** — Understand: I made him so, that he might have the greenness of faith and of works, and always seek heavenly things in his mind.
**“like a … fir tree”** — Septuagint: I am like a thick juniper; from me is his fruit found. Of juniper, according to the Septuagint, Solomon made the doors of the temple; for Christ, through whom we go up to the Father, has this nature, that he always flowers and bears new fruits and never loses his greenness. This juniper gives fruit, rest and fullness to those who rest under its shade, so that they may not be struck by the heat of this world, and so that the heat may not beat on their heads, as once on the head of Jonah.
**“from me is thy fruit found”** — All his work, or the keeping of the New Testament, came from my gift.
14.9:
**“Who is wise”**
• of himself
• In these words the prophet shows the obscurity of the book and the difficulty of explaining it. Who? As if to say: Rare is he who can know all these things, unless they have been explained by the holy fathers, through the grace of Christ who came in the flesh.
**“and he shall understand these things?”** — What do the two women and their childbearing signify, and the other things contained in the prophecy?
**“prudent”** — through others
**“and he shall know these things?”** — namely, this is to be understood of all things: that the ways of the Lord are right
**“for the ways of the Lord are right”** — that is, the commandments of the New and the Old Testament
**“for … are right”** — In these ways no one walks but he who is converted to the Lord, and from whom the veil is taken away that was over the face of Moses, and who says with David: “Open thou my eyes: and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law.” He will walk, and will find Christ.
**“and the just shall walk in them”** — only the just understand rightly and fulfil it in deed
**“but the transgressors”** — The Jews, the heretics, the false Christians, who sin in the law, and will be punished the more heavily through the law.
**“shall fall in them”** — hence: “Behold, this child is set for the ruin, and for the resurrection of many in Israel.”

1.1:
**“The word of the Lord”** — of the Father
**“that came”** — not as regards himself
**“to Joel”** — the name means “beginning,” or “he is God”
**“the son of Phatuel”**
• the name means “breadth,” or “God opening”
• The word of the Lord. Jerome: Pethuel, the father of the prophet Joel, was called Bethuel by the Seventy translators. But since Bethuel means nothing at all in Hebrew, it is better to read Pethuel, which means “breadth” or “God opening.” Hence in Mark: “Ephpheta, that is, Be opened.” And well is Joel, who could say to the people: “Our mouth is open to you, O ye Corinthians, our heart is enlarged,” and who heard from the Lord: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it,” called the son of Pethuel, that is, of God, in whose power it is to open the mouth of man and to enlarge the holy man himself until he comes to perfection. Of this Pethuel, then, Joel is the son, that is, “beginning,” or “he is God”: for he who knows himself a beginner must grow through humility, so that with Moses he may hear: “He who is, hath sent me,” that is, the true God, as distinct from those who are not true gods. To this Joel, then, rightly came the word of the Lord, which was in the beginning with God. Further, it is said to come, not as regards itself, but as regards him to whom it comes; hence: “he is become my salvation.” So the word came, that is, the word spoke to the prophet.
1.2:
**“ye old men”** — That is, you who are ripe in the Lord, who have left infancy behind, understand with the spiritual ear the mysteries I am about to tell; and you, inhabitants of the land, who put your hope in earthly things, if you cannot hear spiritual things, at least take in the literal sense with the ears of the body. The prophet makes an opening in which, by the greatness of what is to be said, he makes the hearer attentive, for he says such things have happened neither in the old history nor in the present age. After the opening follows the narrative: That which the palmer-worm hath left.
**“and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land: did this ever happen in your days, or in the days of your fathers?”** — of those now living
1.3: **“Tell ye of this to your children”** — to all your offspring to come
1.4:
**“That which the palmer-worm hath left”**
• he is worn down by this plague who is overcome by sorrow beyond measure
• The palmer-worm is a worm found mostly among vegetables. The young of the locust before it has wings is called the bruchus; then, when it begins to fly a little, it is called the locust or attelabus; and when it flies fully, it is called the locust. The bruchus is much more harmful than the locust or the attelabus, for, lying in one place, it eats up the fruits to the root. Mildew is when the tender crops are struck by a harmful dew, and both stalk and ears turn the red of vermilion or of ochre. If these come one by one they are harmful; but if they all come together, they carry off everything entirely. And it could have happened historically that all these came together in the times of King Ahab and Elijah, when there was so great a famine for three years and six months that mothers are recorded to have eaten their sons.
• Palmer-worm: a worm of leaves, rolled up in a vegetable or a vine-leaf. It is named from “gnawing off.”
**“the locust hath eaten”** — he suffers from this disease who overflows with too much gladness
**“and that which the locust hath left, the bruchus hath eaten”** — This vice is when we fear adversity beyond measure.
**“and that which the bruchus hath left, the mildew hath destroyed”**
• By this vice we rejoice immoderately over a good to come.
• Mildew: he means rust, which grows from corroded brass.
• Allegorically: By the palmer-worm are signified the Assyrians or Chaldeans, who took captive the ten tribes in the time of Hezekiah, and the two, with the priestly tribe, in the time of Jehoiachin, the grandson of Josiah. By the locust, the Medes and Persians, who, when the empire of the Chaldeans was overthrown, held the Jews captive, though many of the two tribes returned with Zerubbabel by Cyrus’s leave. By the bruchus, the Macedonians and all the successors of Alexander, above all Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, who settled in Judea like the bruchus and devoured all that the former kings had left; under him were the wars of the Maccabees. By the mildew, the Romans, who utterly laid waste all Judea, overthrew its cities, burnt the temple of the Lord, and carried off the whole people by famine, sword and captivity.
• Those who are wrapped in these disturbances cannot look upon the light of wisdom.
*Jerome:* In the moral sense: By these four are signified four passions of the mind, which, if they rule beyond measure, take away the soul’s salvation. Two are of the present: sorrow at present adversity, and joy at present prosperity. Two are of the future: fear of evil to come, and hope of good to come. But the strong man ought so to bear himself that he neither rushes into any evil through present or hoped-for prosperity, nor is troubled beyond measure by present or future adversity. Otherwise: I think the palmer-worm is the passion as it begins in the mind, which is slow and cannot run about, and by stubborn lingering drinks up all the greenness. If we do not kill it in ourselves, it grows and flies, and now devours whatever it touches, now leaves things half-eaten and goes on to others; and, returning to its former seat, it becomes the bruchus, so that by its slowness it devours not only the leaves and bark but the pith. And if, as rarely happens, some breath of life remains after the bruchus, the mildew lays everything waste, turning even the stubble and the worthless hay black, so that they are useful neither for food nor even for dung.
*Gregory:* By the palmer-worm he marks lust, by the locust vainglory, by the bruchus the greed of the belly, by the mildew anger. For many tame lust, but are then lifted up into pride; from pride they fall into gluttony; from too much eating and drunkenness into anger and fury.
1.5:
**“Awake, ye that are drunk”**
• you who lie in the depths of vice
• Ye that are drunk, who put your pleasure in delightful things and turn your mind from all that is profitable: for it is cut off, understand: the wine, that is, the sweetness and your delight, God doing this, so that those who did not know God in prosperity may be forced to know him in adversity, and those who abused riches may be forced by want to return to the virtues.
**“Awake”** — Having set down the harmful passions, since they lie in the dregs of luxury and of every error, he warns those who lie there to rise from their vices and obtain God’s mercy by the tears of penance; or, according to the history, so as to be set free from the captivity of their enemies.
**“and weep, and mourn”** — nothing so makes drunk as the disturbance of the mind
**“all ye that take delight in drinking sweet wine”** — Vices are sweet while they are done, and honey drops from the lips of a harlot; hence honey is not offered in God’s sacrifices.
**“for it is cut off”** — the past for the future, for in the prophet’s time the captivity was still to come
**“from your mouth”** — The old men ought to understand it of spiritual drunkenness, which leads a man to death; the inhabitants of the land should take in with their ears what is said of the wine in which is luxury. Let him who is sunk in drunkenness wake up and weep that he has been drunk, so that his weeping may be turned into laughter, and he may rejoice that he no longer has the stuff of drunkenness, which by its abundance had made him drunk and mad.
1.6:
**“For a nation is come up upon my land, strong”** — whom human effort cannot resist
**“For a nation”** — He shows through what the wine and the rejoicing perished: namely, through the nation of the locusts. And the Jews think that in this prophet’s time locusts laid everything waste historically.
**“and without number”** — What is more numberless than locusts?
**“his teeth are like the teeth of a lion: and his cheek-teeth as of a lion's whelp”**
• whom he compares to locusts in their multitude and to a lion in their cruelty; he compares their kings to lions, their princes to lion’s whelps, with whom a numberless multitude comes
• By the metaphor of the locusts he signifies the coming of the enemy, namely, of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Medes and Persians, and at last the Romans. And it is to be noted that the fierceness of the enemy is so told under the figure of the locusts that he compares the locusts themselves to the enemy; so that when you read of locusts you think of the enemy, and when you have thought of the enemy, you come back to the locusts.
• Allegorically: The nation of the princes of this world and of darkness comes up upon the land of God, that is, the human soul; for every soul of man is the land of God. Hence: “As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine.” The teeth of this nation are like the teeth of a lion, for “your adversary, the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about, seeking whom he may devour.” The lion’s whelp is the Antichrist, or a perverse doctrine. If this nation comes up upon us, at once it lays waste the vineyard, that is, the heart, from which ought to come the wine that gladdens; and it peels off the bark of our fig trees, so that we have not the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, and so that the holy man may not rest under our fig tree or vine while he fears the onset of the adversaries. Nor is that enough for this nation, unless it searches out and kills whatever is alive, so that, all the greenness consumed, the little branches remain white and dead, and that is fulfilled in us: “If in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?”
1.7:
**“He hath laid”** — this nation
**“my vineyard”** — which I brought out of Egypt and planted
**“waste, and hath pilled off the bark of my fig-tree”** — the people of the Jews, in which the hungry Saviour found no fruit, and so cursed and withered it
**“he hath stripped it bare”** — He keeps to the metaphor of the locusts.
**“and cast it away”** — their goods, by plundering; some by taking them captive, some by killing them
1.8:
**“Lament”** — O people of Israel
**“like a virgin”** — laments
**“Lament like a virgin”** — As a young bride who loses her bridegroom in the flower of his youth girds herself with sackcloth and weeps, so the prophet urges the Israelites likewise to weep for the loss of the almighty bridegroom, whom they lost from the time they worshipped idols in Egypt. This people was a virgin in the patriarchs and prophets, by virginity of mind, and by the knowledge and worship of the true God; but after the idols it became an adulteress. Yet even this harlot the bridegroom takes as his wife in Hosea, bringing her, that is, out of the filth of the Gentiles. This can be said of any soul: if it has believed God from its earliest age, it has God for its virgin bridegroom; if anyone returns to the light of faith from among the Jews or pagans or heretics, he has a bridegroom indeed, but not a virgin one.
**“girded with sackcloth”** — haircloth
**“for the husband of her youth”** — who in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob espoused to himself a virgin defiled by no idolatry
1.9:
**“is cut off”** — for, “because iniquity hath abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold”
**“Sacrifice”** — of fine flour
**“Sacrifice … is cut off”** — As regards the history: when the fields and vineyards were laid waste by the nations signified by the four creatures, the sacrifice ceased, which is of the more solid things, such as barley, wheat and flesh, and the libation, which is of liquids, such as wine and oil. When these were taken away, the priests mourned, because those things were not being offered on whose tithes they lived.
**“and libation”**
• of wine
• A libation is only of the cup; to make libation: to pour out.
**“from the house of the Lord”** — the Church
**“have mourned”** — above all because the tithes were not being offered
**“the priests”** — who are
**“ministers”** — of the altar
*Jerome:* All these things can be seen to have happened among the Jewish people for the sin of Christ’s Passion, when Jerusalem was laid waste by the Romans with famine and sword, and all joy and all the observances of the law failed. Daily too, when the Church, founded by Christ’s teaching, is separated from the bridegroom by sin, there perishes in it the sacrifice of an afflicted spirit and the wine that “may cheer the heart of man”; and as iniquity abounds, the teachers of the Church grieve that the virtues fail and the vices increase: for there fails the wheat of faith, the wine of spiritual understanding, the oil of mercy, and the barley of simplicity, or of keeping the letter. These are laid waste by the four mentioned before: lust, vainglory, the greed of the belly, and anger. So the universal Church laments, that she may receive comfort from God.
**“the Lord's”**
• for
• All things were either fruitless, or, if fruitful, were consumed when the locust laid them waste; and so all these things happened, that joy might be taken away from the children of men.
1.10:
**“The country is destroyed”** — The land of the Jews was laid waste at the coming of the enemy.
**“the ground hath mourned”** — the inhabitants of the ground
**“for the corn is wasted, … is confounded”** — taken away from them
**“the wine”** — of which it is said: “my chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it!”
**“hath languished”** — has failed
**“the oil”** — of which it is said: “let not oil depart from thy head”
1.11:
**“are ashamed”** — as the fruit of the virtues fails
**“The husbandmen”** — the preachers
**“the vine-dressers have howled for the wheat, and for the barley”** — by which the weak are sustained
**“have howled”** — For while they held the crops of the harvest and vintage in their hands, the hostile nations came and took away everything they should have lived on, and destroyed them themselves by famine and sword.
**“because the harvest of the field is perished”**
• all that the ground is wont to bring forth
• The harvest of the Church: virtues, reward, works.
1.12:
**“The vineyard”** — which, when it should have brought forth grapes, brought forth wild grapes
**“is confounded”** — trodden down by the multitude of the enemy
**“and the fig-tree hath languished”**
• is become withered
• under which Nathanael was before he believed
**“the pomegranate-tree”** — The pomegranate, to whose rind the cheeks of the bride are compared in the Canticle; it is a healing tree, whose fruits are red and bitter to eat. It is called malogranatum (“grained apple”) because its fruit has many grains.
**“and the palm-tree”** — “The just shall flourish like the palm-tree.”
**“and the apple-tree”** — “as the apple-tree among the trees of the woods”
**“and all the trees of the field are withered”** — the fruit-bearing as well as the fruitless
**“all the trees”** — All things bear the scourge of man, for whose sake they were made.
**“because joy is withdrawn”** — that is, troubled and taken away
**“from the children of men”**
• the Jews
• therefore
1.13:
**“Gird yourselves”** — understand: with the sackcloth of penance
**“Gird”** — Let the holy priests who eat the Lord’s pasch be girded with the belt of chastity; hence: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands.” Let the sinners, whose conscience gnaws them, be girded with haircloth, that they may lament their own sins and the people’s.
**“and lament, O ye priests, howl, ye ministers of the altars”** — not with a feigned but with a pure heart
**“go in”** — into the Church by penance, from which you went out by sin
**“lie in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God”** — make up for the riches by which you have offended with severity of life, so that you can soften God’s anger; and I command this because … is cut off
**“because sacrifice and libation is cut off from the house of your God”**
• unless you repent, you will perish
• The priests are urged to lament first, so that, as the people sinned when they sinned, so it may repent when they repent.
1.14:
**“Sanctify ye a fast”** — for it is not enough otherwise to take the habit of penance, unless the fast is adorned with other good works, and unless one abstains from all unlawful things
**“call an assembly”** — a synod
**“gather together the ancients”**
• who, near to death and ripe in knowledge, take on the fear and worship of God the more
• The right order: first the wise, afterwards those who cling to earthly things; hence above: Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land.
**“all the inhabitants of the land”** — understand: gather together
**“into the house of your God”** — which is the Church
**“and cry ye to the Lord”**
• all together
• with mouth, heart and deed
• Not long after, the captivity of both the ten and the two tribes came, by the Assyrians and by the Chaldeans. It is foretold to come so that, when it came, it might not be thought to have happened by chance or by the cruelty of the enemy, but by the wrath and threat of God; or surely so that, if the people did penance, what was to come might not come. All these things can be referred to the day of judgment, of which retribution all the prophets write. Hence Isaiah: Behold the day of the Lord shall come, past healing, in which is eternal damnation.
1.15:
**“Ah, ah, ah”** — Three times, because they had offended the Trinity
**“for the day”** — for the retribution
**“because the day of the Lord is at hand, and it shall come like destruction from the mighty”** — by whom all things are ordered
1.16:
**“Is not your food cut off before your eyes”** — the food you hoped for, in which you ought to have lived, is taken as it were out of your hands in your presence
**“Is not”** — Food: the wheat of the spirit, the barley of the letter; for sinners suffer, according to the quality of their sins, a famine of the word of God; and so in consequence joy perishes, so that those who ought to have heard from the Apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always,” now hear from the Lord: “Blessed are they that mourn.”
**“from the house of … God”** — moreover, which is graver
**“our”** — is cut off
**“joy and gladness”**
• for sacrifice is no longer offered there
• All these things can be understood under the metaphor of the palmer-worm, the locust, the bruchus and the mildew: namely, that when the crops were taken away and laid waste, famine and pestilence took possession of everything.
1.17:
**“The beasts have rotted in their dung”** — When food and joy are taken away, those “whose God is their belly” fail in their luxury and idolatry and gluttony, and end their life there.
**“are destroyed”** — because the wheat that was stored is lacking
**“the barns”** — where the wheat was laid up
**“the store-houses are broken down”**
• the cellars
• that is, hearts, or earthly abundance
• Store-house: a barn.
• Barns and store-houses are in vain where wheat and wine fail.
1.18:
**“Why did … groan”**
• when all things have fallen, then they will groan for want of good things
• Or the cattle groaned when everything was dried up for the sins of men.
**“the beast”**
• not man, not the image of the living God
• And why?
**“why did the herds of cattle low?”** — “He is compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them.”
**“because there is no pasture for them”** — of eternal life
1.19:
**“To thee, O Lord, will I cry”** — my people will cry through me
**“To thee … will I cry”** — When he has told the evils that were to come, the prophet speaks to God in his own person and the people’s.
**“because fire hath devoured”** — what fire is wont to do to stubble and flame to brambles, this the palmer-worm, the locust, the bruchus and the mildew do
**“the beautiful places of the wilderness”** — the level plains, or meadows, or any places green with grass, which gave pasture to the cattle
**“and the flame hath burnt all the trees of the country”**
• so that the crops and fruits perished
• It is to be noted that neither the prophet nor the people would cry to the Lord except through the taking away of their delights. This can be referred to a man once just, who, when he has turned aside from justice and done evil, his former virtues will not profit him, but God will judge him in what he finds him in. Mystically, the wilderness figures the Gentiles, bereft by idolatry of the flower of the virtues. Or according to the saying: “for many are the children of the desolate, more than of her that hath a husband,” the beautiful places of this wilderness, that is, good works and virtues, the fire, that is, the devil, devours, as flame consumes stubble. But against these arrows of the devil we must cry like a thirsting garden bed, that the dew of divine mercy may quench them. Otherwise, by the springs that are dried up can be understood the teaching of Christ, which is dried up in those who have withdrawn from God, by the fire of lust, vainglory, gluttony and anger.
1.20:
**“Yea, and the beasts of the field”**
• not the prophet alone, or the people through the prophet
• not men only
**“have looked up to thee, as a garden bed that thirsteth after rain”**
• they looked up in terror, begging for mercy
• As a garden bed longs for rain, so all those beasts, worn down by thirst and hunger, cried to the Lord.
**“for the springs of waters are dried up”**
• drunk up and drained by the multitude of the enemy
• “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water.”
**“and fire”** — the laying waste by the locusts
**“hath devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness”** — all the pasture of the field

2.1:
**“Blow ye the trumpet”**
• So that all the people in Jerusalem may hear and fear.
• O prophet, you and your companions, preach openly the coming of Nebuchadnezzar, or of the Romans.
**“in Sion”** — In the Church; hence above: “Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion.”
**“Blow ye the trumpet in”** — The voice of God to the prophet and to the others who kept the law; and again, by the metaphor of the locusts, the onset of the Chaldeans is described.
**“sound an alarm in my holy mountain”**
• in the temple that I have sanctified for myself, or in Christ
• so that
**“let … tremble”** — through penance
**“all the inhabitants of the land”** — given over to earthly things
**“because the day of the Lord cometh”**
• Cry this: that the day of the Lord cometh.
• of the last captivity, or of judgment, or of each one’s end
**“because it is nigh at hand. A day of darkness, and of gloominess, a day of clouds and whirlwinds”** — and it will not be put off
**“because it is nigh at hand. A day”** — On which the light of joy will be taken from the Jews by the Chaldeans, for everything was full of punishments and torments; or for those condemned in hell too, the gloom of darkness is kept.
2.2:
**“as the morning”** — As the rising dawn first takes the mountains, so judgment will begin from the high and mighty, so that “the mighty shall be mightily tormented.” Or, according to the letter: as the morning quickly puts the darkness to flight, and the dawn lights up the mountains, so the army of the Babylonians will be spread over your land.
**“a numerous and strong people”** — Understand: so will it come and be spread over the mountains and valleys of the Jews.
**“a … people”** — Of the Chaldeans, lest you think it a feeble crowd; or the people of the angels, that I may render to each according to his works.
**“the like to it”** — The Assyrians were not stronger than the Romans, nor Nebuchadnezzar stronger than Alexander, the greatest of kings. So it is to be understood thus: there was no nation like the Assyrians, nor king like Nebuchadnezzar, from the beginning, namely, since kings began to be; nor shall be even to the years of generation, that is, until Alexander, who first reigned over all Greece; and generation, that is, until the time of the Romans.
**“nor shall be after it even to the years of generation and generation”** — No punishment can be compared to that which will be on the day of judgment.
2.3:
**“Before the face thereof a devouring fire”**
• “For our God is a consuming fire,” who will burn up wood, hay and stubble.
• Before the face etc.: He describes the coming of Nebuchadnezzar, who will consume whatever he touches like a devouring flame; for whatever nation heard the report of him melted away for fear, and when he had passed over it, he devoured everything like fire, leaving nothing whole.
**“and behind it a burning flame”** — so as to leave nothing unpunished
**“the land is like a garden of pleasure before it”** — which he has not touched, where he will find nothing to burn
**“like a garden”** — As paradise is filled with every delight, so the land of the Jews was full of all good things before he laid it waste; but he reduced it to a wilderness. Hence he adds: Neither is there any one that can escape it.
**“and behind it a desolate wilderness”** — which he has touched, he will reduce to ash and embers
**“neither is there any one”** — Zedekiah and his princes tried to flee from him, but they were caught by his army; and when his princes had been killed, Zedekiah was blinded and led to Babylon in a cage like a lion.
2.4:
**“The appearance of them is as the appearance of horses”** — of the palmer-worms, the locusts, the bruchus, the mildew
**“and they shall run like horsemen”**
• to torment those they have received into their power
• Like horsemen: it is not the Babylonians that are compared to horsemen, but the locusts. By a figure, the enemy’s horsemen are said to run hither and thither.
2.5:
**“like the noise of chariots”**
• Understand: is heard.
• Or: like the noise of chariots, so will be the noise of the locusts. They shall leap upon the tops of mountains, so as to climb all the heights.
**“like the noise”** — So, understand, the noise and terror of their voice will lay everything waste, and they will lay everything waste as flame does stubble.
**“upon the tops of mountains”** — longing to torment all the lofty, and those set on the summit of the Church
**“They shall leap”** — So the locusts themselves will leap.
**“like the noise of a flame of fire devouring the stubble”** — So they will come ready to punish.
**“as a strong people prepared”** — So they will come prepared.
**“to battle”**
• the locusts; and yet, while we read of locusts, we understand the Babylonians
• When locusts are sent by God, they make so great a noise that their sound can be heard from the sixth milestone, as those hand down into whose borders they are wont to come.
2.6:
**“At their presence the people shall be in grievous pains”**
• So great will be everyone’s terror, so great the consciousness of their sins, that no one will shine, no one will have the brightness of joy.
• At their presence etc.: that is, at the presence of the army of locusts the peoples will be tormented, and all faces, understand, of the Jews, will be made like a kettle, which, set on the fire, is covered with blackness and soot.
**“all faces shall be made like a kettle”** — for fear
2.7:
**“like valiant men”**
• Understand: men.
• When the Chaldeans come to the gates of Jerusalem, each one goes in by the way by which he first came to the wall, making himself an entrance in the wall.
**“They shall run …: like men of war”** — the locusts, through the land of the Jews
**“they shall scale”** — They will not enter by the gates.
**“the wall”**
• of Jerusalem
• every fortification, nor will the height of the walls hold them back
**“the men shall march every one on his way, and they shall not turn aside from their ranks”** — They shall not turn aside: The locusts, doing the work God has laid on them, will fly in order, and will not turn aside to another part, so that one may not seem to hinder another.
2.8:
**“No one shall press upon his brother”** — He will carry out the punishments entrusted to him against sinners.
**“they shall walk every one in his path”** — fulfilling their own office
**“yea, and … through the windows”**
• The windows are the five senses, through which death came in; through these the enemy longs to enter and take the city of a good conscience.
• He follows out the metaphor of the locusts, to which no place is impassable; for it is said that when locusts are sent by God as a scourge, they not only run over houses and walls, but fly hither and thither through the insides of the houses.
**“they shall fall”** — so that there be no delay when the doors are shut
**“and shall take no harm”** — that is, they will not be weakened
2.9:
**“They shall enter into the city: they shall run upon the wall”** — on your fortifications
**“the houses”**
• of the Jews
• which we shall build with good works
**“they shall climb up …, they shall come in at the windows, as a thief”** — “To shoot in the dark the upright of heart.”
**“they shall come in … as”** — As a thief coming in by the window is wont to steal in secret, so they, when the doors are shut, come in through the windows, not from fear but from headlong boldness, in their greed for plunder.
2.10:
**“At their presence”**
• at the presence of the army of locusts
• At their presence etc.: When at God’s bidding locusts pass from place to place, by their multitude they are wont to shut out the sun’s rays from the earth and overshadow it like a cloud. By their likeness it is said: when the Assyrians come, so great a dread will seize the Jews in their affliction that not only the earth but also the heaven and all the elements will seem to them to be moved. Otherwise: by the sun can be understood the kings: Jehoiakim the father, and Jehoiachin the son, and above all Zedekiah.
**“the earth hath trembled”** — by exaggeration
**“the heavens are moved”** — “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.”
**“the sun and moon are darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their shining”**
• for even those who are holy will not see the presence of God without dread
• By the moon, the queen; by the stars, the princes of the Jews; for whom, when they were taken by the enemy, everything was turned into darkness.
• The sun and moon etc.: They will not be able to look on such great torments of the wretched, but will mourn, and instead of their bright light they will be covered with dreadful darkness.
• All these things, from the place where it is written: Blow ye the trumpet in Sion, can be referred to the day of judgment, which will be terrible when all the wicked are condemned. Then the heavens and the earth will be moved, and the sun and the moon and the stars will be darkened, as the Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away,” and “the powers of the heavens shall be moved.”
2.11:
**“And the Lord hath uttered”** — will utter
**“And the Lord”** — And the locusts or the Chaldeans will not do this by their own strength, but by the will of God, who at the coming of the enemy will strike the Jews with exceeding terror.
**“his voice”** — In the least of living things too the great power of God is shown.
**“before the face of his army: for his armies are exceedingly great”** — that is, of the demons, who are the armies of God, because they fight for him even against their will
**“for they are strong, and execute his word”** — Hence it is plain that the Babylonians will come by God’s will and obey his command.
**“for the day of the Lord is great”** — of vengeance
**“for … is great”** — From the beginning of this prophecy to this place, where it says: the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, is a threat and a description of what God will bring on a sinful people; from this place to where he says: Why should they say among the nations: Where is their God? is an exhortation to penance.
**“and very terrible”** — even to the good
**“and who can stand it?”** — Which of the Jews could escape the necessity of captivity and death?
**“and who can stand it”** — As if to say: no one, or hardly anyone, will be able to stand the day of judgment who does not give it matter in himself for severity.
2.12:
**“Now, therefore, saith the Lord: Be converted to me with all your heart”** — not only with the lips, but with the whole understanding, will and deed
**“Now, therefore, saith”** — Having foretold the captivity under the likeness of locusts, he invites the Jews to penance, so that they may avoid the evils foretold; as if he said: I have threatened you with all these things so that by the terror of punishment I may bring you to penance for your sin.
**“in fasting”** — that you may be filled hereafter
**“and in weeping”** — that you may laugh
**“and in mourning”** — that you may be comforted
2.13:
**“And rend your hearts”** — Open your hearts by the confession of faith; for they are like wineskins full of sins, and unless they are rent, they will burst of themselves.
**“and not your garments”** — as the Jews were wont to do in a time of sorrow or adversity
**“and”** — so
**“turn to the Lord your God”** — whom their sins have made a stranger
**“for he is gracious and merciful”** — and do not despair if your sins are great, for his mercy is greater, and he “desire[s] not the death of the wicked,” but his penance
**“patient and rich in mercy”** — he does not punish at once, but waits
**“and ready to repent of the evil”**
• granting mercy over evils, after penance
• Evil, that is, the affliction of the penitent; according to that saying: “Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof”; and: “Shall there be evil in a city, which the Lord hath not done?” But because he had said: God is merciful and patient, lest the greatness of his mercy make them careless in doing penance, the prophet adds: Who knoweth? As if to say: I urge you to penance, I preach God’s mercy; but since we cannot fathom “the depth … of the wisdom, and of the knowledge of God,” I hope for the sentence rather than presume upon it.
2.14:
**“Who knoweth”** — as if to say: it is either impossible or hard to know, so it is safer to do penance
**“but he will return”** — from wrath to mercy
**“and forgive”** — our sins
**“and leave”** — that is, grant
**“behind him”** — that is, after his scourge and vengeance
**“a blessing”** — the forgiveness of sins
**“sacrifice”** — hence: “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise: and pay thy vows to the most High.”
**“and”** — and, having received forgiveness, we shall offer
2.15:
**“Blow the trumpet in Sion”** — preach penance publicly in the Church
**“Blow the trumpet”** — The divine word urges the preachers and prophets to preach penance before the enemy’s sword comes; as if to say: Above I warned you to penance, both by recalling the cruelty of the enemy and by recalling my mercy; but now again and again I command: Blow.
**“sanctify a fast”** — by good will, prayer and deed
**“call an assembly”** — a synod, or a gathering
2.16:
**“Gather together the people”** — so that the people who wandered away from God, scattered, may be gathered into one and please God
**“sanctify the church”** — so that there be none in it but the holy, lest “a little leaven corrupt the whole mass”
**“assemble”** — Septuagint: choose
**“the ancients”** — not so much in age as in wisdom
**“assemble the ancients”** — Those who are old only in age are bidden to assemble, so that at least at the last end of life they may repent; those old in conduct and knowledge, so that they may give others example and teaching.
**“gather together the little ones”** — to whom it is said: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat”
**“and them that suck at the breasts”** — “Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise.”
**“them that suck at the breasts”** — Let there be no age that is not converted; for there is no one on the earth, not even an infant of one day, without sin: if he is not held by actual sin, he is held by original sin.
**“let the bridegroom go forth from his bed, and the bride out of her bride-chamber”** — so that in the time of fasting they may not give themselves to the marriage act, but be free for prayer
2.17:
**“Between the porch”**
• that is, the porch that clothes the inner house, a place fitting for penance and confession
• There were two altars: one in the temple, called the altar of incense; the other in the porch before the doors of the temple, called the altar of holocausts. Hence it is said: between the porch and the altar, in the space that is between the altar of incense and the altar of holocausts.
**“and the altar the priests, the Lord's ministers, shall weep”** — who ought to “weep with them that weep” and move others to weeping
**“the priests … shall weep”** — Saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is scandalized, and I do not burn?”
**“and shall say”** — he teaches what the priests ought to say, and how they ought to entreat God
**“Spare, O Lord, spare”** — forgive their sins
**“thy people”** — thine now, because it repents; before, while it sinned, not thine
**“and give not thy inheritance”** — “Israel is my inheritance”
**“to reproach”**
• so that they serve the nations
• namely
**“that the heathen should rule over them”** — which are compared to the palmer-worm, the locust, the bruchus and the mildew, which said to the captives: Why does your God not help you?
**“the heathen … over them”** — The demons, who rule over us while we are unrepentant, and say: Where is their God?
**“Why should they say among the nations”** — that is, why dost thou let it be said by the peoples?
**“Where is their God?”** — whom they thought their defender
2.18:
**“The Lord hath been zealous”** — that is, God first avenged and scourged his people, but afterwards, appeased by their penance, spared his people
**“hath been zealous”** — As if to say: when the people and the priests had done what was said before, God loved his land, which before he had despised.
**“for his land”** — the soul, in which God sows good seed
**“and hath spared his people”**
• Allegorically: Every soul is the land of the Lord, in which he sows. But if it brings forth cockle, it offends the Lord. If it repents and says: Spare, O Lord, the Lord is zealous for his land, and deigns to speak to it, saying: I will send you corn and wine.
• The Lord hath been zealous for his land: that is, he will spare it, which he had long despised.
2.19:
**“And the Lord answered and said to his people”** — not so much to their words as to their deeds
**“And … answered”** — When the people does penance, God spares them so far as to make them worthy of his answer; this we see happen daily in the Church.
**“Behold I will send you corn”** — “the bread … which came down from heaven”
**“Behold I”** — I, who sent upon you when you sinned the palmer-worm, the locust, the bruchus and the mildew, by which all your crops were laid waste, am now turned to mercy by your penance; and I will rescue you from the Assyrians, and if you persevere in good, I will fill you with all good things.
**“and wine”** — which “may cheer the heart of man”
**“and oil”** — which may “make the face cheerful”
**“and you shall be filled with them”** — so that the old sorrow of their sins may be tempered by the gladness of the corn, the wine and the oil, that is, of the virtues
**“and I will no more make you”** — as captives
**“a reproach among the nations”** — From this place to: and my people shall not be confounded for ever, is the promise of good things to those who have done penance.
**“among the nations”** — Among those, namely, of whom it was said above: a numerous and strong people. Or among the nations, that is, the demons; hence: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood: but against principalities and power, against the rulers of the world of this darkness: against the spirits of wickedness.”
2.20:
**“And … the northern enemy”** — that is, the people of the Assyrians, who dwell in the regions of the north
**“the northern”** — According to the letter, it is not the north wind but the south that is wont to bring locusts: for they come not out of the cold but out of the heat. But because he was speaking of the Assyrians under the likeness of locusts, he puts in the north, so that we may understand, not real locusts, but the Assyrians and Chaldeans. Hence: “From the north shall an evil break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land.”
**“I will remove far off from you …: and I will drive him”** — if he comes
**“into a land unpassable, and desert”**
• into some nation forsaken by God
• in which the Holy Spirit does not dwell
• which has no knowledge of God
**“his face”** — According to the letter, this was done to the Chaldeans in the time of Hezekiah, when in one night a hundred and eighty thousand were struck by the angel in their camp; and that part of the camp was killed which faces towards the eastern sea, that is, towards Sodom, and the hinder part, which faces towards the sea that leads to Egypt. Since their bodies were consumed by fire and turned to earth, what follows about the stench is to be understood, not of the bodies of the Assyrians, but mystically.
**“towards the east sea”**
• I will turn him, so that his first part falls into the eastern sea
• Towards the sea: Mystically, in those who opened to him the door of sin, towards the eastern sea, among whom the Assyrian, that is, the devil, remains to the end of their life.
**“the east sea”** — Where Sodom once was, and the other cities that were turned into the sea that is called Dead, because no living creatures live there.
**“and his hinder part towards the utmost sea”** — I will turn his last part towards the uttermost sea, which is to the west and leads to Egypt, on whose shore are Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Joppa, Caesarea and other cities.
**“and his stench shall ascend”** — And his stench shall ascend upon those who promise themselves great things and fall through pride; lest frail man be secure, let him fear falling the more, the more he grows in virtues.
**“and his rottenness shall go up, because he hath done proudly”** — upon them
**“and … shall ascend”** — He keeps to the metaphor, and speaks according to the lie of the province, so that he seems to speak of locusts and not of enemies. For Jerome says that in his time a swarm of locusts covered all Judea; and afterwards, by God’s mercy, between the porch and the altar, that is, between the place of the cross and of the resurrection, as priests and people cried: Spare, O Lord, spare thy people, a wind rose and they were thrown headlong into the first and the last sea; and when heaps of the dead were washed up out of the waves onto the shores of both seas, a rottenness and a harmful stench came out of them, and, corrupting the air, brought a pestilence on men and beasts.
2.21:
**“Fear not”** — having threatened above, he now promises prosperity, and turns tears into laughter
**“O land”** — of promise, which hadst lost God’s seed by thy dryness
**“be glad, and rejoice: for the Lord hath done great things”** — mercy to thee, so that even the beasts are multiplied for thee, which above we read were worn down by hunger and thirst, and the wilderness is filled with glad tilled land
2.22:
**“Fear not, ye beasts of the fields: for the beautiful places of the wilderness are sprung, for the tree”** — of the cross, or according to the letter
**“hath brought forth its fruit”** — the Holy Spirit
**“the fig-tree, and the vine”** — the word of God
**“have yielded their strength”** — their bounty
2.23:
**“And you, O children”** — spiritually
**“of Sion”** — of the Church
**“rejoice, and be joyful”** — after penance, you who before were strangers
**“in the Lord your God”** — not in other things
**“because he hath given you”** — will give
**“a teacher of justice”**
• Septuagint: food
• Christ, who “will teach you all truth”
• Christ
**“and he will make the early … rain to come down to you”**
• the first teaching of the faith
• the old law
• And he will make … to come down: As to the letter, the early rain is that which comes when the crop is sown; the latter, that which comes when the crop is to be gathered. Mystically, the early rain is faith, the latter the perfection of works. Or the early rain is the knowledge of God that is given after faith; the latter, the fullness of the same knowledge.
**“and the latter”** — the New Testament
**“as in the beginning”** — of the blessing
2.24:
**“And the floors shall be filled”** — So great will be the abundance that after you are filled, much will remain on the floors and in the presses.
**“with wheat”** — he will make you abound in the fruits of the virtues
**“and … shall overflow”** — by this word great plenty is signified, so that they may also give others what is left over to themselves
2.25:
**“And I will restore to you the years”** — For as many years as you suffered famine, for so many years again I will double the fruits.
**“which the locust, and the bruchus, and the mildew, and the palmer-worm have eaten”** — I will not let the plenty perish which you lost through the disturbances of the mind.
**“the palmer-worm”** — Which hardly moves and is crushed by a light touch: in this the great strength of God and the frailty of man are shown, as by the gnats in Egypt, which are so small they can hardly be seen. God could indeed have covered everything with a flood or burnt it with lightning, but he shows his power and our frailty by such things. For if these are stronger than man, why is “earth and ashes proud”?
**“my great host”** — Namely the demons, who are the avengers of those who do evil, such as the one who deceived Ahab and the one who troubled Saul. To such tormentors Paul handed over sinners “for the destruction of the flesh.”
2.26:
**“And you shall eat”** — the fruits of justice
**“in plenty, and shall be filled”** — if you persevere in the work you have begun
**“and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God”** — and deservedly
**“and you shall praise the name”** — Novatian and certain other heretics say that a man after sin cannot be restored to his former state by penance. This error is plainly destroyed here, since the Lord receives the penitent so fully that he calls them his people, and declares that they will not be confounded, and that he will dwell in the midst of them, and that they will have no other Lord, but will trust with their whole heart in him, who will abide in them for ever.
**“and my people shall not be confounded for ever”** — if you persevere in the work you have begun
2.27:
**“And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel: and I am the Lord your God, and there is none besides”** — for the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and the Spirit in both
**“and”** — and therefore
**“my people shall not be confounded for ever”** — these things too are promised to the penitent
2.28:
**“And it shall come to pass after this, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh”** — hence Isaiah: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God”; for otherwise it will not see it, unless the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out
**“I will pour out my spirit”**
• This was done on the day of Pentecost. Hence Peter: “For these are not drunk, as you suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day: but this is that which was spoken of by the prophet, Joel.”
• Pouring out signifies the bounty of the gift: for the gifts of the Spirit are not on a few, as in the Old Testament, but on all believers; and on all flesh, because there is no distinction of Jew and Greek, but all who believe are one in Christ.
• He who says he believes in Christ and does not believe in the Holy Spirit has not yet clear eyes to see the salvation of God. Hence those baptized by John in the name of him who was to come, that is, of the Lord Jesus, because they said: “We have not so much as heard whether there be a Holy Ghost,” are baptized again; or rather they receive true baptism. For without the Holy Spirit and the mystery of the Trinity, whatever is received in one person or another is imperfect.
• Since Peter said this prophecy was fulfilled at the time when the Lord suffered, we must see how what follows can fittingly be compared with what went before. For since there came first, from the beginning of the prophecy, the threat God made to a sinful people, and after the threat the warning to penance, and after the warning comes the recalling of the rewards God will give in the future, there seems to be a confusion of order in what is put here in the middle, about the things that were done at the time of the resurrection, which were also given as the reward of faith. Some say that the things promised generally for the last time are now fulfilled in part; and because the apostles felt the reward of things to come at the first coming, both Peter and the other apostles recall certain first-fruits of wonders fulfilled, so that, until “that which is perfect is come,” we may feel what has gone before in part. Some say it is the apostles’ custom to confirm, by testimonies from another time, whatever they saw to be useful to their hearers and not against present things; not so as to abuse the simplicity and ignorance of their hearers, as Porphyry lies, but, according to the Apostle, they preach “in season, out of season”; and, following the rule of the prophets, they say that whatever the Jews carnally promise themselves for the last time was fulfilled spiritually at the Lord’s first coming.
**“shall prophesy”** — afterwards, not at once
**“your sons”**
• Agabus prophesied in Caesarea, and in Antioch there were many prophets, and the four daughters of Philip the evangelist prophesied
• who are of greater merit
**“and your daughters”** — who are of lesser
**“your old men shall dream dreams”**
• of more advanced age
• Paul was old when it was said to him: “Pass over into Macedonia.”
**“and your young men shall see visions”**
• who overcome the evil one
• Paul was young when he was blinded on the road, and afterwards, in ecstasy, was caught up into paradise and heard secret words
**“your young men”** — Or young men, that is, believers, will understand visions, that is, prophecies.
2.29:
**“Moreover, upon my servants and handmaids in those days”** — who still have the spirit of fear, which “perfect charity casteth out”
**“Moreover, upon”** — They will not indeed prophesy, nor dream, nor see visions, but, content with the outpouring of the Spirit alone, they will preach the grace of faith and salvation.
**“I will pour forth my spirit”** — when I am raised from the dead
2.30:
**“And I will shew”** — Wonders were given in heaven at the time of the Nativity, when a new star was seen, and of the Passion, when the sun was darkened, so as not to see the Lord hanging on the cross, or so that his enemies might not enjoy its light. On earth he gave signs: it trembled when he died, and by that unwonted movement the rocks were split and the tombs opened.
**“wonders in heaven”** — Signs
**“and in earth, blood”** — when, Christ being already dead, his side was opened, and blood and water flowed out against nature; hence: “Why then is thy apparel red?”
**“and fire, and vapour of smoke”** — this fire has light in believers, and darkness in unbelievers, which is called vapour of smoke
**“and fire”** — That is, the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on the apostles at Pentecost and gives daily in baptism; this fire enlightens believers and consumes vices. By the vapour is understood the compunction of tears; hence some, compunct in heart, said to the apostles: “What shall we do, men, brethren?”
2.31:
**“The sun shall be turned into darkness”** — not that it was changed into darkness, but that it brought darkness on the world
**“and the moon into blood”** — although the evangelists do not record this, yet we believe it happened according to the letter
**“and the moon”** — Or the moon was not turned into blood historically; but it condemned the Jews, covered with the horror of their blasphemies and their denial of Christ, by the eternal blood of their own testimony, when they said: “His blood be upon us, and upon our children.”
**“before the great and dreadful day of the Lord doth come”** — The day of the resurrection, which is great for the believing elect, dreadful for the devil and all the reprobate. Before this day the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, while the Lord hangs on the cross. Or this remains to be done before the day of judgment, which is so great and dreadful that on it even “the pillars of heaven” are said to “tremble.”
2.32:
**“And it shall come to pass, that every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved”** — by believing and doing; which belongs to the perfect, who believe with the heart, confess with the mouth and fulfil in deed. Otherwise, “not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.”
**“for in Mount Sion, and in Jerusalem shall be salvation”**
• spiritual
• From Sion went out the apostles and the first Church, for three thousand believed on one day and five thousand on another, and afterwards many thousands; of whom Isaiah: “Except the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we had been as Sodom.” And though they are many thousands, he calls them the residue, and as it were a remnant called by God, because they are few in comparison with those who remained in unbelief. Allegorically: the beginning of those who are saved is in the watchtower and the vision of peace.
**“for in Mount”** — Sion is the tower, Jerusalem the rest of the city; hence: “the law shall come forth from Sion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem”; of which it is also said: “it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem.”
**“as the Lord hath said”** — speaking in this prophecy through Joel
**“and in the residue whom the Lord shall call”** — We must see that we refer all these things in the figurative sense to the time of the Passion and Resurrection, as Peter and Paul referred them. For it cannot be that we understand what went before of the time of the Passion, and what follows of the day of judgment, since the later things are joined to the former, and all are done at one time; which what follows shows: For behold in those days etc.

3.1:
**“For behold in those days”** — When salvation has been brought about in Sion and Jerusalem, as the day of judgment now draws near, I will convert to the faith the Jews who were taken captive for their unbelief, at the preaching of Elijah and Enoch; “and so all Israel should be saved,” not only of the two tribes but of the ten as well. And when this has been fulfilled, I will gather the nations. Some understand this childishly: that the Lord will come down to judgment in the valley on the side of the Mount of Olives. This is idle, for he will sit, not on the earth, but in the space of this air, over against the place of the Mount of Olives from which he ascended; and, as John Chrysostom says, the angels will carry the sign of the cross before him. Josaphat means “the judgment of the Lord.” So to the Lord’s judgment there will be gathered, not only the Jews who would not believe, but all the wicked who have been from the beginning of the world. But the just will not go down into the valley of judgment, that is, of damnation, but “shall be taken up … in the clouds, to meet Christ.”
**“For behold in those days, and in that time when I shall bring back the captivity of Juda, and Jerusalem”** — After I have preached sight to the blind and deliverance to the captives, and set free those who confess the Lord and who live in the Church, in which is the vision of peace, I will gather all the nations that would not believe and bring them down into the valley of Josaphat; that is, I will drag them down from the heights to the depths. For everyone who is judged for his sin is put in the valley that is called Josaphat, that is, the judgment of the Lord. For “he that believeth in him is not judged: but he that doth not believe, is already judged,” that is, condemned.
3.2:
**“I will gather together all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Josaphat”** — All these things can be referred to the Assyrians and Chaldeans, who will be condemned at the judgment for the evils they brought on the Jews; who, though we read that they were sent by God to punish the Jews, are yet justly condemned, because they ascribed the victory not to the power of God but to themselves. These words can also be referred to the heretics and proud teachers, who scatter by wicked word and example, and lead into the rites of the Gentiles. The prelate puts the boy in the stews and sells the girl for wine who sees men entangled in lust and other vices and does not rebuke them, for the sake of shameful gain.
**“and I will plead”** — that is, I will judge
**“with them there for my people, and for my inheritance, Israel”** — Convincing them, not by the might of my majesty, but by the truth of reason; them who have divided my inheritance by divers errors.
**“whom they have scattered among the nations”** — where, after the manner of the Gentiles, some worshipped Jupiter, others Juno, and the like
**“and have parted my land”** — so that one part of the land served one god, another another: Crete Jupiter, Thrace Mars
3.3:
**“And they have cast lots upon my people”** — how many of them the king should take as menservants and maidservants, and how many each prince
**“and the boy they have put in the stews”** — so that against nature they worked shame upon males
**“and the girl they have sold for wine, that they might drink”** — putting gluttony and the greed of the belly before lust, abusing boys in place of women
3.4:
**“But what have you to do with me, O Tyre, and Sidon”**
• understand: is there in common, that you always attack me in my inheritance
• But what etc.: The Jews think this is said against Tyre and Sidon and the Philistines, because in the time of the Jewish captivity, when the Jews were conquered by the Romans, they persecuted the people of God, or rather God in his people. So they maintain that the vengeance for the blood of Christ, and the overthrow of Jerusalem, which happened by God’s judgment, came upon Tyre and Sidon on their behalf.
• Tyre and Sidon, cities of the Gentiles, joining with the Philistines who lived in Palestine, often afflicted the people of God; so the Lord will rebuke them. Tyre means “straitness,” and they straitened the people of God; Sidon “hunting,” and they hunted the people to death.
